ModHarness-RL: Recasting Harnesses as Learnable
and Evolving Programs for Agentic RL

Zelin He    Siyu Zhu    Jacob Helwig    Yujian Liu   
Li An    Rohit Jain    Shiyu Chang    Alborz Geramifard Website
Abstract

Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly relies on a harness, the scaffold around the model that decides what it sees of its own interaction and what guidance it receives. Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL, which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State, a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model’s context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During RL training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories, so the harness tracks how the model’s behavior shifts. We study CodeSearch in depth and further analyze ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, with models from 1.5B to 8B. The proposed Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings. These results suggest that a harness for agentic RL can be learned from the task’s data and evolved with the model.

 ModHarness-RL

1 Introduction

Large language models now act as autonomous agents that solve tasks through multi-turn interaction with external environments (Yao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024b). Agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which trains these agents directly from verifiable environment rewards, has emerged as a promising paradigm  (Jin et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025; Da et al., 2025). A harness, the engineered layer between the environment and the model, governs what the model reads and how its behavior is guided. One line of work compacts the growing transcript of the interaction through memory, summarization, and pruning  (Packer et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Bashir et al., 2026; Shao et al., 2026), while another guides behavior through added instructions, interfaces, and guardrails  (Yang et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2025). Agentic RL has begun to train models under such harnesses, but the harness is typically hardcoded for a specific task and held fixed throughout training  (Jin et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2024). This leaves two challenges. First, an effective harness must be tailored to the task, the data, the model, and the context budget, and tuning one by hand for every such configuration does not scale, so it should be derived from data instead. Second, the effective harness keeps changing as the model trains. RL resolves some failures on its own, so new harness components should be added only for the failures that persist. This leads to a natural question. How can a harness be made optimizable from data, and then optimized with the model training?

Recent efforts have begun to adapt the harness during RL, by decaying fixed rubric scaffolds on a preset schedule (Zhou et al., 2026), alternating task-specific scaffold rewrites with weight updates (Hebbar et al., 2026), or editing planning, action and memory modules from observed faults (Chen et al., 2026a). Yet their update spaces are fixed in advance or tied to a task-specific scaffold, so adaptation reduces to selection or revision within an engineered space. None provides a general way to derive harness operations from the typed states of the interaction and optimize them alongside the model.

In this paper we propose ModHarness-RL, a method that exploits the modularity of an agent’s interaction to learn the harness from its trajectories and evolve it with the model. It is built around two questions.

  • •

    How should a harness be represented to be learned and evolved? To learn a harness from data, we first need a representation of it that defines what can be searched and evolved, and we need to narrow which of its components to search. ModHarness-RL represents the harness as programs over a structured State, which records the interaction as typed blocks such as each turn’s reasoning, tool call and tool result. These blocks are the building blocks from which ModHarness-RL assembles the context and control. We focus on two core components, both written as programs over them. A Compression program reassembles the blocks into organized model context under a fixed budget, and a Steering program reads them to detect when behavior deviates and appends guidance. Programs over these blocks have three properties that suit learning and evolving. They are (1) learnable, since an LLM can write them directly from training trajectories and their corresponding rewards; (2) computationally inexpensive, allowing them to be run on every turn of every trajectory without calling another model, so Compression can optimize the context at scale; and (3) testable, allowing each candidate harness to be replayed over stored trajectories to evaluate its fitness before it is accepted or rejected.

  • •

    How can the harness be learned and evolved with the model? As training progresses, model behaviors change. Failure modes from previous model versions may become less frequent, while new ones may emerge. ModHarness-RL therefore uses an end-to-end pipeline that updates the harness from online data. It summarizes experiences from training trajectories, proposes and verifies candidate programs, and validates them on held-out training tasks. To evolve the harness with the model, we alternate this pipeline with RL updates of the model weights. The key insight is that the harness should guide only what the model cannot learn on its own. Therefore, we propose a Replay mechanism, which reruns each candidate Steering program over trajectories from past training steps and installs it only for the failures that persist as the model trains.

We train models from 1.5B to 8B with GRPO in three environments (CodeSearch, ALFWorld and BIRD SQL), each under different context budgets. On CodeSearch, ModHarness-RL improves over the fixed-harness baseline by 14 to 24% in every setting and scores highest against memory, skill, prompt and harness evolution baselines, by 5 to 12% over the strongest of them. On ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, each program alone improves over the base harness in seven of eight settings. We also investigate a series of research questions, from the score and token use of Compression and its comparison with frontier model-based compaction, to an ablation of each Steering component.

2 Preliminaries

Multi-Turn Agents. An LLM agent with policy πθ\pi_{\theta} solves a task q∼𝒟q\sim\mathcal{D} by interacting with an environment over multiple turns through a set of tools 𝒯\mathcal{T}. At turn tt the agent reads a context ctc_{t}, samples an action at∼πθ(⋅∣ct)a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c_{t}), its full response for the turn ending in a tool call, and receives an observation ot=𝒯⁡(at)o_{t}=\mathcal{T}(a_{t}), continuing until a terminal turn TT. The harness builds the context ctc_{t}, including any guidance the agent receives, from the task and the interaction so far.

Agentic Reinforcement Learning. The agent is trained to maximize the expected reward of its trajectory τ=(q,a0,o0,…,aT)\tau=(q,a_{0},o_{0},\ldots,a_{T}), that is maxθ⁡𝔼q∼𝒟,τ∼πθ​[r⁡(τ)]\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D},\,\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}[r(\tau)], where r⁡(τ)r(\tau) is the reward that the environment assigns to the trajectory. In this paper, we optimize this objective with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024; Section A.1).

3 Learning and Evolving the Harness as Programs in Agentic RL

We introduce ModHarness-RL, which learns the harness from data and evolves it with the model as the model trains with RL. It represents the harness as programs over the typed blocks of a structured State for two core components (Section 3.1), and learns and evolves these programs with the model.

3.1 Representing the Harness as Programs over State

As the agent interacts with the environment, we record each turn as an action and observation pair ui=(ai,oi)u_{i}=(a_{i},o_{i}) and take the State to be the task together with the turns so far, st=(q,u0,…,ut−1)s_{t}=(q,u_{0},\ldots,u_{t-1}). We store sts_{t} as a typed record, like an instance of a Python class, where each turn has attributes for the reasoning the model wrote (.thought), the tool call (.name, .args), and the result (.exec_output, or retrieved documents with their own typed metadata), plus any guidance shown on that turn (Figure 2, left). A basic harness renders this record directly as one growing transcript, appending every turn,

ctflat=flatten⁡(st)=q⊕u0⊕⋯⊕ut−1,c_{t}^{\mathrm{flat}}=\operatorname{flatten}(s_{t})=q\oplus u_{0}\oplus\cdots\oplus u_{t-1}, (1)

where ⊕\oplus denotes concatenation. This append-only context leaves two problems, and we address each with a program over sts_{t}.

compress

As the interaction accumulates, a high volume of irrelevant tool outputs may obfuscate the small fraction of decision-relevant evidence (Liu et al., 2024a). compress reads the blocks of sts_{t} and returns a new view of the State that keeps the key information and fits the budget. It re-renders earlier turns and offloads what is no longer needed (Figure 2, ).

steer

Without any intervention, models sometimes show recurring mistakes (Yang et al., 2024). steer is a set of triggers, each paired with a short piece of guidance. A trigger is a small program over sts_{t} that fires on one detectable failure mode, such as a repeated tool call, and steer returns its guidance as a block only on the turns where it fires (Figure 2, ).

Together the two programs form the harness we learn, ℋ=(compress,steer)\mathcal{H}=(\hbox{\pagecolor{compressbg}{compress}},\ \hbox{\pagecolor{steerbg}{steer}}). The rest of the harness, such as the tool set and the action format, remains fixed as each environment defines it. In place of ctflatc_{t}^{\mathrm{flat}}, the harness renders the new view of the State that the two programs produce,

ct=flatten⁡(compress​(st)⊕steer​(st)),c_{t}=\operatorname{flatten}\bigl(\hbox{\pagecolor{compressbg}{compress}}(s_{t})\oplus\hbox{\pagecolor{steerbg}{steer}}(s_{t})\bigr), (2)

where the guidance is appended after the compressed turns and is empty on the turns when no trigger fires. Both programs read the full record sts_{t} at every turn, so what one turn offloads stays available for building later contexts. Executing ℋ\mathcal{H} calls no model and costs no model tokens, so it runs on every turn of every trajectory at scale. See Appendix D for concrete examples.

3.2 Evolving the Harness with the Policy

With the harness represented as programs, we can build these programs from the policy’s own rollouts, so that they are tailored to both the task and the policy, and keep evolving them over training (Figure 3, Algorithm 1).

3.2.1 Optimizing the Compression Harness

Verbose tool outputs waste context tokens and distract the model from decision-relevant evidence, limiting performance. The compression optimization performs a data-driven search for a program that retains only the spans of tool outputs driving task performance. We fit compress once before training and hold it fixed, so that the context the policy trains on stays stable. While we also explored refitting compress as the policy trains, we found that holding it fixed scores higher (Table 3).

Rollout. We roll out the base policy π0\pi_{0} on the training tasks 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} under the append-only context of Equation 1, keeping each trajectory with its reward and grouping them by task. The result seeds the reservoir ℛ0=Rollout​(π0,𝒟train)\mathcal{R}_{0}=\textsc{Rollout}(\pi_{0},\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}).

ProposeCompress. The rollouts are fed to an LLM creator. The creator reads these rollouts, along with how their contexts filled up, and writes several candidate compression programs. Each candidate is then refined in a loop. The creator compiles and repairs each candidate until it runs, applies it to stored episodes from ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0}, and computes two measurements. One checks whether the program is unfaithful, removing task-relevant information, and the other checks whether it is inert, leaving the context largely unchanged. The creator accepts the candidate or revises it, and the last version of each candidate forms the proposal set 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

Gate. Each program in 𝒫\mathcal{P} gets one trial on the held-out training tasks 𝒟trainhold\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{hold}} under the frozen base policy, with the same agent loop, tools and context limit that training will use. The best becomes ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} and is held fixed for the rest of training.

3.2.2 Evolving the Steering Harness with the Policy

Steering optimization guides the policy only on the failures it cannot learn to fix during training. These failures change as the policy trains, so steer is updated every round.

UpdatePolicy. We train πk−1\pi_{k-1} with GRPO on 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} under the incumbent harness ℋk−1\mathcal{H}_{k-1}, which yields the updated policy πk\pi_{k} together with the rollouts ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k} it produced along the way, and those rollouts join the reservoir.

ProposeSteer. ℛk\mathcal{R}_{k} records what the current policy can and cannot do, so the creator reads its mixed-outcome groups, the tasks on which some rollouts succeed and others fail, and proposes failure hypotheses from them. Each hypothesis carries a trigger, a small program over sts_{t}, together with the corrective insight its guidance will be written from. The proposed triggers form the proposal set 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

Replay. The newest rollouts show what is failing now, but not whether the failure will persist. It may be an incidental error that the policy learns to avoid with further training, or a stable failure that it will not fix on its own. Because each trigger is a program, we can classify the failure type retrospectively. We execute every candidate hypothesis over all stored rollouts ℛ0:k\mathcal{R}_{0:k} and record how often its failure occurs at each training step. Replay needs no model call, so it stays computationally inexpensive however large the reservoir grows. The resulting curves show the trend of each failure over training, whether it is falling, holding steady or rising, and the curves of all triggers together give the replay evidence ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Admit. A judge reads each trigger’s replay evidence together with its guidance and the installed set, and returns one of three verdicts: (1) intervene when the failure holds steady or rises, installing the trigger and its guidance; (2) monitor when it looks real but has not settled, keeping the trigger for another round without showing guidance; or (3) continue when it keeps falling.

Gate. The admitted triggers are gated together, since guidance interacts, and accepted as ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} only if they score strictly above ℋk−1\mathcal{H}_{k-1} on the held-out training tasks 𝒟trainhold\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{hold}} under πk\pi_{k}.

4 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate the performance and efficiency of ModHarness-RL on three agentic environments (Section 4.2), and then study its two harness modules through three research questions (Section 4.3).

4.1 Setup

Environments.

In CodeSearch (Sutawika et al., 2026) the agent localizes a bug in a real repository by naming the file, module and entity to edit. We train on SWE-Smith and evaluate on SWE-Bench Lite, Verified and Pro, scoring the mean F1 of the three names on [0,1][0,1]. In BIRD SQL (Li et al., 2023) the agent queries a real database to answer a natural-language question. We train on the BIRD training split and evaluate on its dev split. In ALFWorld (Feng et al., 2025), a text-world household environment, the agent completes a household task through a sequence of actions. We train on the training games and evaluate on the held-out seen and unseen games. In all three, evaluation uses tasks never seen in training. 𝒟trainhold\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{hold}} is held out from the training split and is disjoint from every evaluation set.

Methods.

Every method shares the environment, the policy and the training configuration, and differs only in what surrounds the model. “Base harness” is the hand-written scaffold, unchanged throughout training; “++ Compression” and “++ Steering” add one learned program each and nothing else; ModHarness-RL runs both, with Compression learned once and Steering evolving with the policy. The baselines take one representative of each component that can be learned alongside a policy, namely memory, skills, prompts and the harness itself. EvolveR (Wu et al., 2026) learns memory, retrieving from an experience base distilled from past rollouts. SkillRL (Xia et al., 2026) learns skills, inducing a reusable library of them. INSPO (Zhou et al., 2025) learns prompts, co-evolving task instructions with the policy. HarnessForge (Chen et al., 2026a) learns the harness, editing planning, action and memory modules from observed faults. DeepAgents (LangChain, 2026) is the fixed-scaffold control, an elaborate hand-written harness with a planning checklist, a scratchpad and sub-agents.

Models and training.

CodeSearch uses Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B and BIRD SQL uses Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B, both with reasoning disabled, and ALFWorld uses Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Qwen2.5-1.5B is warm-started with supervised fine-tuning before RL (Appendix A). We choose the model family for each environment so that RL training shows a clear signal, as with other choices the model either barely learns with RL or saturates. Every method trains with GRPO under an identical configuration for 200 steps on one node of eight H100s, and every metric is computed using the final checkpoint. The K=20K=20 Steering rounds are spaced evenly over training and run beside it, so the trainer never waits for them. For a fair comparison, every method that learns from rollouts uses GPT-5-mini as its creator. It writes the programs of ModHarness-RL, the memory of EvolveR, the skills of SkillRL, the prompts of INSPO and the harness edits of HarnessForge.

Context regimes.

To evaluate the effect of the harness under different context budgets, we set a history budget, the token allowance for accumulated interaction, and run every environment and model under two budgets. We call one model under one budget a setting. In a context-limited setting, the interaction history is capped at a token limit that runs out partway through a typical episode in every environment, so the harness drops or compacts earlier turns. In a context-sufficient setting, the token limit is almost never reached. The specific token limit depends on each setting, so we defer it to Section C.2.

4.2 Main Results

Table 1 reports the full CodeSearch results. ModHarness-RL improves over the base harness by 19% on average, and the gain holds at the file, module and entity level (Table 5). It also beats zero-shot GPT-5-mini, the creator of its harness, in every setting, so the gain is not distillation from the creator. Figure 4 applies each program alone to the base harness, and we can see that the gain from the two programs differs by domain. On CodeSearch, Steering improves over the base harness by 15% on average over the four settings, which is better than Compression at 6%. On ALFWorld under a limited budget, averaged over the two models, Compression improves by 22%, which is better than Steering at 16%. On BIRD SQL, the two are close with Qwen3.5-2B, and with Qwen3.5-4B, Compression performs better.

In Figure 6, we also report the inference time, the average seconds an episode takes end to end, for Qwen3-8B, and show that every method on the frontier is ours except INSPO under the limited budget, which is also fast but scores below the base harness. Section 4.3 further examines these gains.

4.3 Analysis

The gain from Compression. To investigate the gain from Compression, we consider how it improves the base harness in both performance and efficiency. We measure performance with the score of each benchmark and efficiency with prefill tokens. Counting the prompt tokens alone would favour any method that rewrites the history, because a rewritten history can break prefix-cache reuse, and a cached prefix costs the server nothing to recompute. We therefore count prefill tokens, the prompt tokens an episode sends multiplied by the share the prefix cache misses, summed over its model calls. We measure them by replaying the recorded episodes with no turn dropped, so the base harness keeps its full cache reuse but is not held to the budget (Section C.4).

Figure 6 shows that Compression improves the base harness in two ways, depending on the context regime. Under a limited budget, performance tends to improve, with 8% improvement for Qwen3-8B on CodeSearch and 21% improvement for Qwen2.5-7B on ALFWorld. Under a sufficient budget, Compression consistently reduces the prefill tokens. Specifically, under the budget used in training, the prompt at an episode’s last model call is within 3% between the two arms under a limited budget, and Compression uses 74% fewer tokens on ALFWorld and 10% fewer on CodeSearch under a sufficient one. Even though rewriting the history can lose some prefix-cache reuse, Compression still uses fewer prefill tokens: because compress is a deterministic program, earlier turns keep an identical rendering, so the majority of its cache stays valid.

Comparison with compaction by a strong teacher model. A natural alternative to compiling a program is standard compaction, which calls a teacher model to rewrite the history whenever the budget fills. We use GPT-5-mini, the same model that writes Compression. This is a strong baseline, because the teacher is utilized online in every episode and adapts to the content of the episode. In comparison, Compression uses the teacher once, offline, to write a deterministic program that every episode then runs without a model call. Compression scores higher than compaction in 2 of the 4 settings of Table 2 and up to 5% lower in the other two, with on the order of 100×\times reduction in teacher-model calls and tokens over a training run in our estimates (Section C.3) and, in our estimates, greater than 1,000×\times reduction in wall clock time per turn in the context-limited settings, showcasing the efficiency of the compression program.

Ablation of ModHarness-RL. Table 3 ablates each component of ModHarness-RL. Each component improves performance.

Without generation, the creator proposes no new triggers during training, and the policy trains with one Steering program fixed in advance. Without judging, every proposed trigger goes to the gate instead of only those the judge admits. Each lowers the score in every setting, so neither the creator nor the judge carries the result alone.

We then ablate co-evolution by running the two stages one after the other, interchanging the order across two experiments: policy optimization first under a fixed harness, followed by harness optimization under the final policy, and vice versa. Both orders reduce performance in every setting, demonstrating the value of co-evolution.

Finally, ModHarness-RL fits compress once against the base model (Section 3.2). Evolving Compression instead refits compress every ten steps as the policy trains. Results show a dip in performance compared to ModHarness-RL, suggesting the importance of keeping context stable during policy training.

Does the judge know when Steering is needed? Partway through CodeSearch training, the judge reads how often one failure has occurred so far and decides whether to install guidance for it. We continue training from that point both with and without the guidance (Figure 7). In Case 1, the failure keeps recurring, and the judge installs the guidance, which cuts the failure. In Case 2, the failure is already rare and still falling, so the judge holds off, and indeed, without the guidance, the failure keeps falling as training continues. Figure 12 gives the full version.

Case studies. Figure 7 shows one learned compress program and one learned steer trigger as high-level pseudocode. Appendix D (Figures 13 and 14) gives the details and applies both to episodes.

5 Related Work

We discuss the two lines of work closest to ours and defer the broader literature to Appendix B.

Harness and Context Optimization during Training. A line of recent work updates the harness together with the weights, either by letting an LLM agent rewrite the harness code (Chen et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026a; Hebbar et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026) or by training the policy with RL to manage its own context (Shao et al., 2026). These approaches rely on a model to rewrite the harness or to operate on the context directly. ModHarness-RL instead writes harness components as programs over typed blocks that capture rich interaction, which run without a model call, keep the KV cache largely reusable and can be rerun over stored trajectories.

Co-Evolving Memory, Skills and Prompts during Training. Another line of work evolves what the agent reads together with the policy. It distills experience into a memory (Wu et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026), induces, writes or retires skills and guidance (Xia et al., 2026; Ge et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Qi et al., 2026), or evolves task instructions (Zhou et al., 2025), with some methods withdrawing this guidance as the policy improves (Shi et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026). These methods only append to the prompt, and their guidance is retrieved by semantic similarity, matched to the task type or selected by a model. ModHarness-RL instead conditions its guidance on typed blocks, so each trigger can be replayed and targeted at a specific failure, enabling more targeted and deterministic control.

6 Conclusion

ModHarness-RL treats the harness of agentic RL as programs that are learned from data and evolved with the model. It records the interaction as State and writes two harness components as programs over these blocks, Compression, which builds the model’s context, and Steering, which supplies guidance. During training, ModHarness-RL proposes candidate programs from recent trajectories, verifies them by execution, and replays them over past trajectories. Across three environments and two context budgets, each learned program improves over the fixed-harness baseline in nearly every setting, raising the score when context is scarce and reducing prefill tokens when it is not. On CodeSearch it also outperforms memory, skill, prompt and harness evolution baselines.

Limitations

Scope of the comparison.

We investigate CodeSearch most thoroughly, running the full method and the third-party baselines under both a limited and a sufficient budget with two model sizes, to establish the signal. ALFWorld and BIRD SQL then test whether each program generalizes to other environments, again under both budgets and with two model sizes. Ideally the full method and baselines would also cover ALFWorld and BIRD SQL.

Gate sample size.

The gate scores each candidate on a limited set of held-out training tasks, so it can occasionally accept a program that is slightly worse. A larger held-out set would make the gate more reliable, at a higher cost.

Proprietary creator.

The programs are written by a proprietary model, GPT-5-mini. To enable a fair comparison, every learning baseline uses the same creator. GPT-5-mini writes the Compression and Steering programs of ModHarness-RL, the memories, skills, prompts and harness edits of the baselines, and the summaries of the compaction baseline. For ModHarness-RL, the policy sees only the output of executing these programs (Appendix D shows examples). This text is never a loss target, and the programs of ModHarness-RL are built once and can then be reused.

What deterministic programs can capture.

The harness is a set of deterministic programs over sts_{t}, so it captures only patterns that an explicit rule over the recorded interaction can detect and act on, such as a repeated tool call or a tool result whose structure shows what to keep. It suits interaction that is structured and verifiable, such as tool calls with typed results, and is less effective for open-ended interaction such as conversation, where the relevant signal is semantic and hard to detect with a rule.

Ethical considerations

This work trains and evaluates language model agents on publicly released benchmarks for code localization, embodied household tasks and text-to-SQL. No other personal data was collected or used, and it involves no human subjects. The harness programs are generated by a language model and executed in the training loop, so they are compiled and run under a restricted policy before installation rather than executed as arbitrary code.

Appendix A Experimental Details

A.1 Environments and Training

Shared setup. All runs train with GRPO [Shao et al., 2024] in verl [Sheng et al., 2025], and vLLM [Kwon et al., 2023] serves the policy for training and evaluation. Each run uses FSDP with parameter and optimizer offloading for the policy, and a tensor parallel size of one for the policy server. Within an environment, every method uses the same model, training data apart from 𝒟trainhold\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{hold}}, agent loop, tools, reward and optimization settings as the base harness, so the methods differ only in the harness around the model. We take the optimization settings of each environment from the work we follow for that environment, as given below, and keep them unchanged for every method and both context regimes. Every run trains for 200 steps and is evaluated at its step-200 checkpoint. Every method that writes programs, memories, skills, instructions or harness edits uses GPT-5-mini to write them, accessed through the Azure OpenAI Service. We note that the models train slowly with reasoning enabled, so in every environment we suppress reasoning and let the model write a short rationale before each action.

Training objective. For each task qq, GRPO [Shao et al., 2024] samples a group of GG trajectories {τi}i=1G\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} from the current policy and normalizes their rewards Ri=r⁡(τi)R_{i}=r(\tau_{i}) within the group to form advantages,

A^i=Ri−mean⁡({Rj}j=1G)std⁡({Rj}j=1G).\hat{A}_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\operatorname{mean}(\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})}{\operatorname{std}(\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})}. (3)

The policy is updated by the clipped surrogate

ℒGRPO​(θ)=1G∑i=1G1|τi|∑t=1|τi|min(ρi,tA^i,OPENclip⁡(ρi,t,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​A^i)−β𝔻KL[πθ∥πref],\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)={}&\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|\tau_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|\tau_{i}|}\min\!\Big(\rho_{i,t}\,\hat{A}_{i},\\ &\qquad\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i,t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\,\hat{A}_{i}\Big)\\ &{}-\;\beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}\!\left[\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}\right],\end{split} (4)

where ρi,t\rho_{i,t} is the token-level importance ratio, ϵ\epsilon the clip range, β\beta the KL weight, and πref\pi_{\text{ref}} a fixed reference policy.

CodeSearch. We follow the setup of CodeScout [Sutawika et al., 2026]. Each task gives the agent a repository checked out before a fix, together with the issue that the fix resolves, and asks it to name the files, modules and entities that the fix changes. We train on tasks from SWE-Smith [Yang et al., 2025] and evaluate on 288 tasks, 100 from SWE-Bench Lite, 100 from SWE-Bench Verified [Jimenez et al., 2024] and 88 from SWE-Bench Pro [Deng et al., 2026]. We use Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B. Each step samples 8 tasks and 8 episodes per task, and makes one policy update on the whole batch. We use a constant learning rate of 10−610^{-6} with no warmup, a low-variance KL loss with coefficient 0.0010.001, no entropy bonus, and a sampling temperature of 1.01.0 during training. The policy generates at most 1,024 tokens per turn and takes at most 10 turns per episode, with one tool call per turn. A tool call is a shell command that times out after 30 seconds, and the agent observes at most 10,000 bytes of its output. The reward is the sum of the F1 scores of the predicted files, modules and entities against those the gold patch changes, which lies in [0,3][0,3]. We report the mean of the three F1 scores, which lies in [0,1][0,1].

ALFWorld. We follow the setup of GiGPO [Feng et al., 2025]. Each game places the agent in a text-rendered household with a goal from one of six task types [Shridhar et al., 2021]. After each action the agent observes the result of the action and the list of actions that are admissible next. We train on the training games and evaluate on the 274 evaluation games, 140 from the seen split and 134 from the unseen split. We use Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Before RL, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct wins none of the ALFWorld training games, so every GRPO group has zero advantage and gives no gradient. We therefore warm-start it with supervised fine-tuning on 288 games won by ALFWorld’s built-in rule-based expert (9 steps of 32 games), and RL then proceeds identically for every arm. Each step samples 16 games and 8 episodes per game, and makes one policy update on the whole batch. We use a learning rate of 10−610^{-6}, a low-variance KL loss with coefficient 0.010.01, an entropy coefficient of 0.0010.001, and a sampling temperature of 0.60.6 during training. The policy generates at most 2,048 tokens per turn and takes at most 50 turns per episode. The reward is 11 when the game is won and 00 otherwise, with no penalty for invalid actions. Unlike GiGPO, which shows the policy only the two most recent turns, we keep the full history of the episode in the prompt and let it grow until it reaches the context limit, so that training matches a multi-turn setting in which the history accumulates.

BIRD SQL. We follow the setup of MTIR-SQL [Xu et al., 2025]. Each task gives the agent a natural-language question, the full schema of its database and the evidence that BIRD provides with the question, which we place before the question following SQL-R1 [Ma et al., 2025]. We train on the BIRD training split and evaluate on the 1,534 questions of the dev split. We drop the 663 training questions whose task statement alone exceeds 6,144 tokens, which leaves 7,726 questions for training. We use Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B. Each step samples 64 questions and 5 episodes per question, and makes one policy update on the whole batch. We use a constant learning rate of 10−610^{-6}, no KL loss, no entropy bonus and a sampling temperature of 0.60.6 during training. The policy takes at most 6 turns per episode and issues one SQL query per turn. The agent observes the column headers of each query result and at most 10 of its rows. The reward is 11 when the final query returns the same result as the gold query and 00 otherwise.

A.2 Baselines

We implement every baseline on our trainer, so each uses the model, data, agent loop, tools, history budget and optimization settings of ModHarness-RL, with GPT-5-mini wherever the method calls an LLM. All baselines are run on CodeSearch.

EvolveR. Following Wu et al. [2026], GPT-5-mini distills principles from finished episodes into an experience base during training, and the principles retrieved for a task are added to its context.

SkillRL. Following Xia et al. [2026], each skill has a title, a principle and a condition for when to apply it. General skills are always shown, together with the six task-specific skills that best match the task. Every five validation steps, GPT-5-mini adds at most three new skills for each task category that scores below 40%.

INSPO. Following Zhou et al. [2025], we port the authors’ implementation. A population of instructions is placed after the task statement. During training, an instruction is drawn for each episode in proportion to its importance weight, and at evaluation the instruction with the highest weight is used. Weak instructions are removed by successive halving, and GPT-5-mini writes new instructions by reflecting on failed episodes.

HarnessForge. HarnessForge [Chen et al., 2026a] generates an executable harness made of planning, action and memory modules, and then aligns the policy to the selected harness by supervised fine-tuning on trajectories collected under it. Its released code cannot be run on CodeSearch as is. Each benchmark it reports is connected by hand, with its own tool runtime, its own tool loader that requires a sample of that benchmark, and its own scorer, and a generated harness is a Python package built on the agent and provider classes of that code, which call tools through a function-calling interface. We therefore port the loop that evolves the harness and leave out the benchmark-specific parts. Every 50 training steps, which gives three rounds, GPT-5-mini reads training episodes, attributes the most frequent fault to the planning, action or memory module, writes an improvement brief for that module, and proposes an edit, following the first two stages of HarnessForge. We serve a planning or action edit as guidance at a turn, and a memory edit as a rewrite of the interaction history. The policy trains with the same GRPO as every other method in place of the fine-tuning stage.

DeepAgents. We use DeepAgents [LangChain, 2026] version 0.6.12 with its default components, a planning checklist, a virtual file system the agent can write notes to, sub-agents that run a task in a fresh context, and summarization that moves old context to files when the context grows. It is fixed during training.

A.3 ModHarness-RL Settings

ModHarness-RL fits compress once before training and runs K=20K=20 Steering rounds, one every 10 training steps, alongside the trainer (see Section C.1 for a sensitivity analysis). GPT-5-mini at medium reasoning effort writes every program and serves as every judge. Both parts score a candidate against the incumbent with the same policy, on the same 𝒟trainhold\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{hold}} tasks and with the same agent loop, tools and history budget as training, so a difference in score reflects the program and not a change in the policy or the sample.

Held-out training tasks. Both parts of ModHarness-RL choose among programs on 𝒟trainhold\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{hold}}, a set of tasks held out from the training split. We draw 𝒟trainhold\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{hold}} once per environment with a fixed seed and separate tasks by identity, using the issue text in CodeSearch, the game file in ALFWorld, and the database and question in BIRD SQL. The policy of ModHarness-RL trains on the remaining tasks, so no task is both in 𝒟trainhold\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{hold}} and trained on. 𝒟trainhold\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{hold}} has 128 tasks in CodeSearch and ALFWorld. In BIRD SQL it has 128 questions in the context-sufficient settings and 256 in the context-limited settings, where the 256 contain the 128. No program is chosen on an evaluation set, and 𝒟trainhold\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{hold}} is disjoint from every evaluation set we report.

A.4 History Budget and Overflow

We follow the design of verl-agent [Feng et al., 2025], which drops earlier turns from the history and tells the policy that they existed. The history budget applies to the interaction history after compress has run. When the compressed history still exceeds the budget, the harness drops the oldest whole turns until it fits, always keeps the task statement, and marks the gap with the line [earlier turns omitted]. Unlike verl-agent, which always keeps a fixed number of recent turns, we drop turns only when the history exceeds the budget. The rule applies to every method, the base harness included, so the budget is binding on all of them in the same way. This is the dynamic eviction referred to in Section C.4.

Appendix B Extended Related Work

Multi-turn agent learning. ReAct established the interleaving of language reasoning and environment actions [Yao et al., 2023]; AgentBench made the breadth of such interactions visible across environments [Liu et al., 2024b]. Search-R1, WebAgent-R1, Agent-RLVR, RAGEN, and GiGPO train multi-turn tool policies with verifiable outcomes or trajectory-aware objectives [Jin et al., 2025, Wei et al., 2025, Da et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2025, Feng et al., 2025]. Toolformer, ToolLLM, and ToolRL study tool acquisition at different scales [Schick et al., 2023, Qin et al., 2024, Qian et al., 2025]. These methods primarily improve policy parameters or objectives. ModHarness-RL is complementary. It represents the harness as programs over a structured State, and learns and evolves them alongside agent learning.

Context as a managed resource. Agent-computer interfaces can dominate software-agent performance [Yang et al., 2024, Xia et al., 2025]. Position sensitivity and context rot show that nominal context capacity is not the same as usable evidence [Liu et al., 2024a, Hong et al., 2025]. MemGPT treats context as a memory hierarchy, ReSum periodically summarizes search trajectories, Recursive Language Models delegate work over long inputs, and Context-1 trains self-editing search behavior [Packer et al., 2024, Wu et al., 2025, Zhang et al., 2025, Bashir et al., 2026]. These systems motivate our Compression abstraction. ModHarness-RL writes compress as a program over typed blocks, which runs without a model call and keeps the KV cache largely reusable. We fit compress once before training and hold it fixed.

Scaffolds and rubrics. The classical scaffolding view supplies support that can be withdrawn as competence grows [Wood et al., 1976, Vygotsky, 1978]. Rubric-scaffolded RL supplies externally specified reasoning criteria during exploration and decays their use as training proceeds [Zhou et al., 2026]. ModHarness-RL instead conditions its guidance on typed blocks, and its Replay mechanism reruns each candidate Steering program over trajectories from past training steps, and a judge installs it only for the failures that persist as the model trains.

Appendix C Additional Results

This appendix carries the context budget behind each regime, together with the per-granularity (Table 5), per-cell (Figures 9, 10 and 11) and per-step views of the same runs reported in Section 4. Error bars are ±\pm1 SD over ten evaluations of each trained checkpoint on CodeSearch and three on ALFWorld and BIRD SQL.

C.1 Sensitivity to the update interval

Steering runs K=20K=20 rounds over 200 training steps, one every 10 steps. Like the other hyperparameters, this interval is chosen in advance and not tuned. As a small check of its sensitivity, we also train ModHarness-RL on CodeSearch under a sufficient budget with an update every 5 steps (K=40K=40) and every 20 steps (K=10K=10). Table 4 shows that an interval of 10 scores the highest with Qwen3-4B and ties with an interval of 20 with Qwen3-8B.

C.2 Context budgets

The history budget is the token allowance for accumulated interaction, and it is set per cell. It excludes the task description, so tasks with descriptions of different lengths receive the same budget. A context-limited cell sets it to 1,024 tokens, and a context-sufficient cell to 8,192 tokens by default. On BIRD SQL, the 1,024-token budget runs out on 30 to 42% of base-harness turns, dropping earlier turns, while the 8,192-token budget never runs out. CodeSearch uses the same two budgets. ALFWorld episodes run longer than 8,192 tokens, so its context-sufficient budget is raised to 12,288 tokens.

C.3 Cost accounting

In Table 2, Score is measured on the held-out validation set overall, tokens are input plus output, ms/turn is wall clock added to one episode divided by its number of turns, and bold is better within a setting. e is estimated by differencing two runs, s is scaled from a comparable campaign, and b is a lower bound priced at the per-call cost of the setting where that cost is measurable.

C.4 Prefix-cache reuse

A method that modifies the context can break prefix-cache reuse. An append-only harness never changes a token it has already sent, so every prefix stays valid, whereas a rewritten history appears to move under the cache. Compression is a deterministic program, so an earlier turn keeps an identical rendering unless the program changes it, and the cache stays valid for every turn it leaves unchanged. We measure reuse by replaying every validation episode with dynamic eviction removed from both arms, which gives the base harness its best case. The prefill tokens in Figure 6 are the product drawn in Figure 8, the prompt tokens an episode sends times the share the cache misses. Compression serves 58 to 72% of prompt tokens from cache against 64 to 95% for the append-only base, so the rate falls without collapsing, and because it is taken on far fewer tokens the prefill tokens are lower in 3 of 4 cells, by up to 35%. Measured instead as the prompt at an episode’s last model call, served context is within 3% between the arms under a limited budget, and Compression uses 74% fewer tokens on ALFWorld and 10% fewer on CodeSearch under a sufficient one.

C.5 Does the judge know when Steering is needed?

We build a setup to test a single Steering program and its failure rate. Partway through CodeSearch training, the judge reads how often one failure has occurred so far and decides whether to install guidance for it (Section 3.2.2). We then continue training twice from that point, once with the guidance and once without, so that we see the failure rate after both decisions (Figure 12). In Case 1, the failure keeps recurring, and the judge installs the guidance. Installing it cuts the failure. In Case 2 the failure is already rare, and the judge holds off. Without the guidance, the failure still falls as training continues. Installing it would also cut the failure, but it would add guidance for a behavior the policy learns on its own.

Case 1 of Figure 12 trains Qwen3-4B without Compression, and Case 2 trains Qwen3-8B with it.

Appendix D Harness Program Schema and Examples

Figure 13 and Figure 14 show an example compress program and an example steer trigger, each applied to a training episode.

Compression example. Figure 13 applies a generated compress program to a CodeSearch episode. The program shortens only file reads of at least 1,000 characters in earlier turns, replacing each with a digest that keeps the imports, the definitions, and the first and last lines. Search output, short reads and the newest turn are kept as they are. In this episode, the tool output the model reads before turn 5 falls from 5,626 to 2,809 characters, while the structure of the file stays visible.

Steering example. Figure 14 shows a generated steer trigger in a CodeSearch training episode. The check stays silent while the agent searches and opens whole files. After turn 4, the agent’s view shows a single function, so the check fires and the guidance asks the agent to scan nearby definitions before submitting. The agent then widens the view to the function body and submits Term.rlike, which earns the full reward of 3/3 for the correct file, class and function.
